title: Are fortune cookies really Chinese?

sources.cita_corta: Smithsonian National Museum of American History

scenes.narration: In many Chinese restaurants in the United States, the meal ends with a cookie that holds a message. But are they really Chinese?
scenes.image_credit: Fortune cookie broken 20040628 223252 1. User Lorax on en.wikipedia, CC BY-SA 3.0. Wikimedia Commons. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Fortune_cookie_broken_20040628_223252_1.jpg

scenes.narration: Modern fortune cookies have a history tied to Japan and the United States. There are several theories about their exact origin.
scenes.image_credit: Torii path with lantern at Fushimi Inari Taisha Shrine, Kyoto, Japan. Basile Morin, CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikimedia Commons. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Torii_path_with_lantern_at_Fushimi_Inari_Taisha_Shrine,_Kyoto,_Japan.jpg
scenes.visual_description: File:Torii path with lantern at Fushimi Inari Taisha Shrine, Kyoto, Japan.jpg

scenes.narration: A Japanese tradition known as tsujiura senbei used rice crackers with messages. Depictions of this kind of sweet have been found in 19th-century prints.
scenes.image_credit: Fortune Cookie 1878. 孟斉芳虎・画, Public domain. Wikimedia Commons. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Fortune_Cookie_1878.jpg

scenes.narration: In the early 20th century, fortune cookies began to catch on in San Francisco. Makoto Hagiwara, a Japanese immigrant, is one of the figures linked to their spread.
scenes.image_credit: Original Hagiwara fortune cookie press 01. Awkwafaba, CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikimedia Commons. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Original_Hagiwara_fortune_cookie_press_01.jpg

scenes.narration: During World War Two, many Japanese Americans were sent to internment camps. The cookies passed into the hands of Chinese American companies, which made them popular.
scenes.image_credit: Dorothea Lange, Japanese-American boarding up store front before relocation, San Francisco, 1942. Dorothea Lange, Public domain. Wikimedia Commons · original: National Archives / War Relocation Authority (Dorothea Lange). https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Dorothea_Lange,_Japanese-American_boarding_up_store_front_before_relocation,_San_Francisco,_1942.jpg
scenes.visual_description: File:Dorothea Lange, Japanese-American boarding up store front before relocation, San Francisco, 1942.jpg

scenes.narration: That is why, although today they are linked to Chinese restaurants, fortune cookies have Japanese roots and an American history.
scenes.image_credit: Tsujiura senbei. Mark Yasuda, CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikimedia Commons. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Tsujiura_senbei.jpg
